transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, I suppose it’s these little routines I’ve gotten into… nothing dramatic, I don’t think. I’ll wash my hands again after handling my wrist brace, and I find myself rechecking the stove or the front door. Sometimes before I leave, I’ll silently count through the steps in my head.

I know I’ve already done enough, but I still get stuck doing it, and it’s started making me late. I thought maybe I should come in before it gets any more bothersome, if that makes sense.
Do these routines or the need to repeat them cause you anxiety or distress, or do you feel compelled to do them even if you don’t want to?

Yes… I suppose I do feel a bit compelled, though I don’t want to make it sound worse than it is. It’s more like I know I’ve already washed my hands, or checked the stove and the front door, but there’s this uncomfortable feeling if I don’t do it again.

And the counting before I leave… it’s not something I enjoy. I’d rather just go. But if I skip it, I feel unsettled, so I end up doing it, and then I’m late. Does that make sense?

When you feel that uncomfortable feeling or become unsettled, is it because you’re worried something bad might happen if you don’t repeat these actions, or do certain thoughts come into your mind that make you feel that way?

Yes… I think that’s closer to it. It’s not that I truly believe something terrible will happen, exactly, but these unpleasant little thoughts barge in.

I’ll be reading at home, or getting ready for a museum shift, and suddenly I’ll think, “What if I left something unsafe?” or “What if I touched something unclean?” Or even that I might somehow have put someone else at risk. I know, rationally, it’s out of proportion… but it still leaves me feeling I should check or wash again, just to settle it. I hope that answers what you mean.
How much time do these thoughts and routines typically take up in your day, and have they started to interfere with your work or other activities?

It’s not taking over the whole day, I don’t think… I’m still managing on my own, for the most part. But it does add up, especially when I’m trying to get out the door.

I’ve been late to my docent shifts at the museum a few times because I get caught in the checking and counting. And, well… I’ve skipped a few museum events too, not because I didn’t want to go, but because the whole process of leaving started to feel like too much. I suppose that counts as interfering, doesn’t it?
Have you ever tried to resist doing these routines or ignore the thoughts, and what happens when you try?

I have tried, yes. Not in some grand way, but I’ll tell myself, “No, you’ve already washed,” or “You checked the stove once, that’s enough.” And sometimes I can walk away for a minute.

But then I get stuck on it. If I’ve handled my wrist brace, I start feeling like I should wash my hands again. If I’m leaving, I’ll think about the stove or the front door, or I’ll feel I need to count through the steps silently before I go. I know it probably sounds rather small, but if I try to ignore it, I get so unsettled that I usually go back and do it anyway.

And that’s really what brought me in, I suppose. These little routines are making me late, even when I know I’ve already done enough.

Can you describe what goes through your mind just before you feel the urge to wash your hands, check the stove or door, or count silently? Are there specific intrusive thoughts or images that seem to trigger these urges?

Usually it’s just this ugly little thought that barges in, if that makes sense. I might be reading at home, or getting ready to go in for a museum shift, and suddenly I’ll think, well, what if I left something unsafe? Or what if I touched something unclean?

Sometimes it’s more about someone else… like I’ve somehow put another person at risk without realizing it. I do know, perfectly well, that it’s out of proportion. I’m not trying to be dramatic about it. But once the thought is there, it sort of sits in my mind until I wash or check or count through things. Does that answer it properly?

Are these intrusive thoughts that you described something you experience as unwanted and unpleasant, and do you try to suppress or neutralize them by doing the routines like washing, checking, or counting?

Yes… unwanted is the right word, I think. They’re not thoughts I sit there choosing to have. I’ll just be reading at home, or getting myself ready to go to the museum, and this rather unpleasant thought barges in — that I’ve left something unsafe, or touched something unclean, or somehow put someone else at risk.

And I do know, honestly, that it’s out of proportion. I can see that. But in the moment it feels hard to just leave it alone, so I end up washing or checking, or counting through things in my head, as if that will settle it. I suppose that is trying to neutralize it, isn’t it?
How much time do you spend on these intrusive thoughts and the routines you do to manage them each day, and does this affect your mood or ability to focus on other things?

It’s not all day, thankfully. I mean, I am still managing on my own — I don’t want to give the impression that everything has fallen apart.

But it does take up more time than I’d like to admit. Especially when I’m trying to leave the house. I can lose enough time washing again, checking the door or stove, or going through the counting in my head that I’ve been late to my docent shifts. And… I have skipped a few museum events, which is embarrassing to say, because getting out the door just felt like too much.

Mood-wise, it makes me a bit frustrated with myself, I suppose. And it can make it harder to settle my mind onto whatever I meant to be doing next. Is that the sort of thing you mean?
Can you estimate how much time these intrusive thoughts and routines take up in total each day—like how many minutes or hours you spend on them?

I haven’t timed it exactly, I’m afraid. It’s not hours and hours, at least I don’t think so. But on some days it’s enough to interfere with leaving the house.

I’m still managing on my own, really, but the washing and checking and getting stuck counting can make me late for my docent shifts. And I have skipped a few museum events because getting out the door just felt like too much. So… I suppose it adds up more than I’d like to admit.
Can you estimate if the total time you spend on these intrusive thoughts and routines adds up to more than an hour each day?

Yes… I think on some days it probably does add up to more than an hour, though I don’t like admitting that.

It’s the little routines that stretch out — washing my hands again after handling my wrist brace, rechecking the stove and the front door, and then silently counting through the steps before I leave. Each one doesn’t seem like much by itself, but together they can make me late, even when I know I’ve already done enough. Does that answer it properly?
